name: Testicle lumps and swelling: what to check
summary: The NHS says to check your testicles monthly for changes; a lump or swelling needs a GP visit, and sudden severe pain needs A&E or 999.
keyPoints: The NHS suggests checking your testicles about once a month, during or just after a warm bath or shower.
A healthy testicle feels smooth and firm, and one being slightly bigger or lower than the other is common.
The NHS says to book a GP appointment for a lump, swelling, change in shape or feel, or an ache that does not go away.
Most lumps have causes other than cancer, such as hydroceles, cysts, varicoceles or epididymitis.
Sudden, severe testicle pain is an emergency: the NHS says to go to A&E or call 999.
Testicular cancer is one possible cause, and the NHS says it is easier to treat when found early.

body.heading: How do men check their testicles?
body.body:
The NHS suggests checking your testicles about once a month, during or just after a warm bath or shower. The testicles sit inside the scrotum, the bag of skin below the penis.

To start, hold your scrotum in the palm of your hand. Then, with your other hand, roll one testicle at a time between your thumb and fingers. The NHS also describes feeling the tubes at the back of each testicle, called the epididymis. These can sometimes become hard, swollen or painful.

body.heading: What should normal testicles feel like?
body.body:
The NHS says a healthy testicle feels smooth and firm, but not hard. It is common for one testicle to be slightly bigger than the other, or to hang lower.

This means the most useful thing to learn is what is normal for you. Checking regularly makes it easier to notice when something has changed.

body.heading: Which changes are worth noticing?
body.body: The NHS lists several changes to look out for. These include a lump in a testicle, a swollen testicle, or a change in the shape or feel of a testicle. One testicle becoming bigger than the other can also be a change worth noting. So can an ache or pain in a testicle or the scrotum that does not go away. A scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard is on the same list. The NHS stresses that having these symptoms does not mean you have testicular cancer.

body.heading: What else can cause a lump or swelling?
body.body:
The NHS says most lumps and swellings in the testicles turn out to have causes other than cancer. It names several common ones, including varicoceles, hydroceles, epididymal cysts and epididymitis. It also lists a hernia in the groin as a possible cause.

A hydrocele is a swelling of the scrotum caused by a build-up of fluid. A varicocele is a soft lump that develops slowly above the testicle, usually on the left side. An epididymal cyst is a small, smooth, fluid-filled swelling that develops slowly in the epididymis.

Epididymitis happens when the epididymis becomes swollen and painful, often because of an infection. The NHS says it is usually treated with antibiotics. It adds that in men under 35 the cause is usually a sexually transmitted infection, while in men over 35 it is more often a urine infection.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS says to make a GP appointment if you notice a lump or swelling in a testicle. The same goes for a change in the shape or feel of a testicle, or one testicle becoming bigger than the other. An ache that does not go away is also a reason to book an appointment. This is a routine appointment, not an emergency. The NHS still wants these changes checked, even though most turn out not to be cancer.

A GP can look at and feel the testicles and may arrange an ultrasound scan. In Scotland, NHS inform adds that a GP may also shine a torch through the scrotum to look for fluid.

body.heading: Is sudden severe testicle pain an emergency?
body.body:
Yes, the NHS treats sudden, severe pain in a testicle as an emergency. It can be a sign of testicular torsion, where the blood supply to a testicle is cut off. The NHS says this needs treatment in hospital as soon as possible. The route is to go straight to A&E or call 999, rather than waiting to see a GP.

NHS pages also list pain together with sickness or tummy pain, or pain that lasts more than an hour, as reasons to get emergency help. A swollen scrotum or a testicle sitting higher than usual can also go with torsion.

body.heading: Could it be testicular cancer?
body.body:
Testicular cancer is one possible cause of a lump or swelling, and the NHS describes it as rare. Its main signs are the same ones described above, such as a lump, swelling, or a heavy, firm or hard scrotum. Most people with these signs will not have cancer, but a GP is the person to check.

The NHS says testicular cancer is easier to treat when it is found early. This is one reason it encourages men to get to know their own testicles.

If a GP is concerned about cancer, the NHS says you may be referred urgently through the fast-track two-week system. Being referred this way does not mean cancer has been found, only that the NHS wants you seen quickly.
